To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
recombinant human DNAse I does not increase tobramycin antibacterial activity in sputum.
rhDNase did increase the bioactivity (measured as the MIC) of tobramycine in sputum and that the increase was not due to hydrolysis of the sputum DNA.
the bioactivity of the antibiotic tobramycin is not increased by the enzyme DNase I.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms by which sputum inhibits the activity of the aminoglycose antibiotics tobramycin and gentamicin in vitro.
the macromolecular mechanisms of the inhibition of tobraycin activity by sputum
the macromolecular mechanism by which tobramycin is inhibited by sputum and the effect of rhDNase treatment of sputum on the bioactivity of this aminoglycocide.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
rhDNase has no effect on tobramyc in sputum and that tobramycin is bound to sputum by mechanisms other than binding to DNA.
tobramycin does bind to sputum, but that this does not affect its bioactivity.
rhDNase is not a useful agent in the treatment of tobramyc in-resistant P. aeruginosa infections.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
rhDNase is not a potential adjunct therapy to tobramycin.
rhDNase treatment of sputum may not be beneficial to cystic fibrosis patient therapy.
the binding of tobramyacin to DNA is insignificant in sputum and that the binding of this drug to mucin may be the cause of the inactivation of tobramycine in sputum.
The main takeaway from our work is that
sputum inhibition is not due to high molecular weight DNA but to other macromolecules, probably mucins.
the bioactivity of antibiotics in the sputum of CF patients is a function of the macromolecular composition of sputum.
rhDNase may increase the binding of aminoglycoides to sputum.
